name: Fatima Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself and how you came to line work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a logistics coordinator at a shipping firm for sixteen years, booking containers, chasing customs papers, that sort of thing. Around 2024 I watched AI start doing half my job better than me, and when they offered voluntary redundancy I took it, at 41, and walked into a line apprenticeship at the city's electricity company. People thought I'd lost my mind. My husband Tom teaches maths at a secondary school, and we've got Lina, who's twelve, and Max, who's nine. Between the redundancy and some shares my dad left me, we're on solid ground.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a crew that does a lot of live-line work on the city network, which means working on lines that are still switched on, from an insulated bucket, with rubber gloves and sleeves up to the shoulder. I'm not trusted with the live work myself yet, I'm the one on the ground passing up tools, watching clearances and doing the paperwork, and Ray, our crew leader, still double-checks my rigging. Last spring I helped the company trial drone inspections over the industrial park, because I was the only one who'd flown one. I use AI every day, to study, to check procedures, to write up the job notes on the drive back. I love how careful the work is, every step thought through, and what wears me out is how much I still don't know at 43.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, I jumped early and maybe I didn't need to, but I'm happier now anyway. At work I'd laugh with Ray about it, because he thinks I'm a bit of a gadget person. Online I'd probably post something about how the hype cycle fooled everyone, me included.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel slightly silly, because I left a good desk job partly out of fear of this. But I don't regret it, honestly. I like being outside, I like the craft, and the pay is better than I expected once you qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the apprenticeship and aim to start live-line training once I'm qualified. I'd keep using the AI tools for what they're good at, which is study and paperwork. Our money stays invested as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AI Plateau?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, maybe with a little wry smile at myself. Like packing for a storm and getting sunshine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the drone trial go anywhere in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably it becomes a normal tool, like a better pair of binoculars. It's handy for spotting a cracked insulator without climbing, but it doesn't change the job. That's fine with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel slightly silly. Would you say that out loud to Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh, Tom would say it for me. He was the one who said 'are you sure' about a hundred times. I'd let him have that one.

S0.say: She'd say she jumped early and maybe didn't need to but is happier anyway. She'd laugh about it with her crew leader and post that the hype fooled everyone, herself included.
S0.think: She'd feel slightly silly for leaving a good desk job partly out of fear, but doesn't regret it because she likes being outside, the craft and the pay once qualified.
S0.do: Carries on with the apprenticeship and plans to start live-line training once qualified. Keeps using AI for study and paperwork, and leaves the family's investments as they are.
S0.feel: Calm, with a wry smile at herself.
S0.quote: Like packing for a storm and getting sunshine.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima already made one big jump ahead of AI, so the plateau makes her laugh at herself rather than worry. She's comfortable with technology and sees the drone as just a tool. Tom's doubts are a running joke between them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is roughly what I expected, and it's why I moved. At work I'd say we should get ahead of it, ask for training on the drones and the new software before it's forced on us. Online I'd share practical stuff, like which tools actually help in the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think line work is in a good spot. The physical, careful, high-risk stuff stays human for a long time, and the grid needs more of it. And the paperwork side, which I'm good at because of my old job, is exactly where AI helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for every pilot the company runs, drones, tablets, the new planning system. I'd finish my ticket on time and start live-line training. I'd also help Ray and the older guys with the new software, because they'll need it and I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing Steady Disruption?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit pleased even. It feels like I read the weather right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching changes, but it doesn't vanish. Tom already uses AI to make worksheets and mark homework, and he grumbles but he uses it. Kids still need a person in the room making them put their phones away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew might struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bogdan, probably. He's 55, superb on the tools, but he types with one finger and hates screens. If the company makes the job notes digital and he can't keep up, I'd quietly do them with him at the end of the day.

S1.say: She'd say steady change is roughly what she expected and why she moved, and urge the crew to ask for training on drones and software early. Online she'd share which tools actually help in the field.
S1.think: She thinks line work is in a good spot because careful, high-risk physical work stays human and the grid needs more of it. AI helps with the paperwork, which she's good at.
S1.do: Volunteers for every company pilot, including drones, tablets and the new planning system. Finishes her ticket, starts live-line training, and helps older colleagues with the new software.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit pleased, as if she read the weather right.
S1.quote: Kids still need a person in the room making them put their phones away.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima sees steady change as proof her move was right and is eager to lead on new tools. Her care for older colleagues like Bogdan is practical rather than political. She's relaxed about Tom's teaching job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge deal and people need to take it seriously right now, not in a year. I'd be practical rather than angry: here's what you can do this month. At work I'd tell people to look at their savings and keep their skills sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy, but not frightened. I've moved once ahead of AI, and I know I can do it again. And honestly, we've got the shares from Dad, and if the companies building this stuff do well, so do those shares, which is a strange kind of protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd go to the company and ask to be on whatever team deploys and supervises the robots, because I've got the drone experience and the logistics background. I'd look at our investments and make sure some are in the companies that build robots and run power, since the grid is what feeds all of it. And I'd sit with Tom to plan for his job going, probably within the two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of energy. It's like the week before I handed in my notice at the shipping firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Only two years of warning. What does that short time change for you, compared with the slower pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means no long courses, no second apprenticeship. Whatever I do, I do with the skills I already have, so I'd sell myself as the person who understands both the line and the software. In five or ten years I could build something new, but in two I'm using what's in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shares are a strange kind of protection. Does that sit comfortably with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not entirely. It feels a bit like betting on the fire while your neighbour's house is in it. But I'd rather Lina and Max are protected than make a point, and I'd want the government to tax the winners heavily too, me included.

S2.say: She'd say it's a huge deal that needs action this month, not next year, and would be practical rather than angry. At work she'd tell people to check their savings and keep skills sharp.
S2.think: She'd be uneasy but not frightened, having already moved once ahead of AI. Her late father's shares could rise with the companies building AGI, which she sees as a strange kind of protection.
S2.do: Asks to join the team that deploys and supervises the robots, using her drone and logistics experience. Shifts some investments into robot and power companies, and plans with Tom for his teaching job going within two years.
S2.feel: Uneasy but full of energy, like the week before she quit the shipping firm.
S2.quote: It feels a bit like betting on the fire while your neighbour's house is in it.
S2.fieldNote: Secure and adaptable, Fatima treats even two-year AGI as a problem to work, not a catastrophe. She's honest about the moral discomfort of profiting through her shares. Her biggest practical worry is Tom's job, not hers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift if you use it, and I'd tell everyone I know to start now. At work I'd push the company to train its own people for the robot roles. I'd write something sensible online, probably a long post nobody reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to qualify, do live-line work for a bit, and move into running the robot crews. I think the people who'll do well are the ones who know the job and the machine, and that's where I'm heading anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd qualify and keep pushing to be on every pilot. By year two or three, I'd take a course in robotics or automation, at night if I had to, and I'd use AI to get through it faster. We'd rebalance our money gradually, and Tom would start looking at roles in training or school leadership, where a person is still in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Five years is a runway, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep using the word 'pilot'. What would you actually tell the company you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a title and a seat at the table: 'field lead, automation', or whatever they call it. Somebody has to tell the engineers what a real pole in a real back garden looks like. I'd rather that's me than someone who's never been in a bucket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lina about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her what I did: watch closely, move before you're pushed. And I'd tell her it's fine to change your mind at 40, because I did and it was the best thing I ever did.

S3.say: She'd call five years a gift if it's used and tell everyone to start now. At work she'd push the company to train its own people for robot roles, and she'd write a sensible post online.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough to qualify, do some live-line work and move into running robot crews. People who know both the job and the machine will do best, and that's where she's heading.
S3.do: Qualifies in year one and joins every pilot, then takes a robotics or automation course by year two or three, using AI to speed through it. Gradually rebalances the family's investments while Tom looks at training or school leadership roles.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, seeing five years as a runway rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Somebody has to tell the engineers what a real pole in a real back garden looks like.
S3.fieldNote: Fatima has a clear target role and the confidence to ask for it. Her advice to her daughter repeats her own life: move before you're pushed. Five years feels like plenty to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for anybody to get ready, so there's no excuse for anyone, companies, government or us. At work I'd say keep your skills sharp and keep an eye out. I wouldn't make a big fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is almost comfortable. I'd get a full career's worth of line work in compressed form, then shift into the automation side by year five or six. By 53 I'd want to be running something, not being replaced by something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, become a strong live-line worker, then train in robotics around year four. I'd keep investing steadily, and we'd pay off the mortgage early to keep things simple. And I'd help Lina and Max pick studies that mix people with technology, rather than one or the other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing AGI by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is long enough to make it my choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that worries you more than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe complacency. With two years everyone moves, with ten a lot of people will say 'later' until it's too late, and I'd worry about guys like Bogdan doing that. I'd nag him, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said by 53 you'd want to be running something. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small team that maintains and oversees the robots on our part of the network. Me, a couple of people, and a fleet of machines. I'd be fine with that, as long as I'm the one deciding when it's safe.

S4.say: She'd say ten years leaves no excuse for anyone, companies, government or workers. At work she'd tell people to keep their skills sharp and watch closely, without a big fuss.
S4.think: She thinks ten years is almost comfortable: a compressed career in line work, then a move to the automation side around year five or six, so that at 53 she's running something.
S4.do: Qualifies, becomes a strong live-line worker and trains in robotics around year four. Keeps investing steadily, pays off the mortgage early, and helps Lina and Max pick studies that mix people and technology.
S4.feel: Calm, because ten years makes it her choice.
S4.quote: By 53 I'd want to be running something, not being replaced by something.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Fatima's main worry is other people's complacency, not her own position. She pictures herself overseeing a small robot fleet but insists on keeping the safety call. Her outlook is pragmatic and personal rather than political.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, though more for Tom and for people like Bogdan than for me. Two years doesn't give anyone time to retrain properly. What would help is companies training their own workers for the new roles instead of hiring outsiders, and the government taxing the winners, me included if my shares do well, to pay for people while they switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask people whether they've changed careers before. I think that's the biggest thing. Once you've done it once, it stops being terrifying and starts being a plan.

headlineQuote: Once you've done it once, it stops being terrifying and starts being a plan.
portrait: Fatima Schmidt is a 43-year-old apprentice on a city live-line crew who left a logistics desk job at 41 after watching AI do half her work. She uses AI daily, helped trial the company's drones, and has a strong cushion from redundancy pay and her late father's shares. Calm through the plateau and steady change, she stays only uneasy even when AGI arrives in two years, aiming straight for the robot deployment team and worrying more for her teacher husband Tom. With five or ten years she plans to qualify, train in robotics and run a small robot crew. She's frank about the discomfort of her shares gaining from the change and wants the winners taxed, herself included.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mostly for her husband Tom and older colleagues like Bogdan, because two years doesn't give anyone time to retrain properly.
whatWouldHelp: Companies training their own workers for new roles instead of hiring outsiders, and the government taxing the winners to pay for people while they switch.
